blocks.text: It is proved that שממית semamith in Prov. XXX, 28. is neither the ape nor the spider, but the stellio.

Of the four animals whose cleverness Solomon extols in XXX, 28., the last is שממית semamith, which he writes takes hold with its hands, and is in kings' palaces. Over this animal there is a great dispute among the Hebrew doctors. Some explain it as תולעת של מטר, a rain-worm; others as שרץ של כנפים, a winged creeping thing, or שרץ מה מהעופים, some creeping thing of the number of those that fly. R. Jonah explains semamith by the Arabic word خطاف [khaṭṭāf] chottaph, that is, the swallow, as though it were the same as סנונית senunith, as the Chaldeans and the Talmudic doctors call the swallow. This is utterly absurd, since the swallow does not [col. 1084] have hands with which to handle and grasp, nor is it one of the small land creatures with which Solomon deals here: There are four, he says, little things of the earth. So this explanation has nothing sound in it. Aben Ezra, Emmanuel and Kabuenaki, to avoid these difficulties, preferred that שממית semamith be the ape, a most clever animal, a delight of kings, and furnished with hands like a man. But in my judgement it is too large to be counted בקטני ארץ among the little creatures, such as are the ant, the choerogryllius and the locust; for these are the examples Solomon used before. Some press in vain the resemblance of the word semamith to simia [ape]. For the name simia comes from nowhere else than from the simae [snub] noses. That is why the same animals were once called enares [noseless] ^{a)}, and the Πιθηκοῦσσαι [Pithēkoussai] of the Greeks are the Enariae islands of the Latins, as the distinguished Salmasius observes on Solinus. Quite otherwise think R. Levi, Kimchi and Elias: namely, that שממית semamith is the spider, which is accustomed to dwell in the towers of kings as much as in the huts of the poor, and there to weave its web with such skill of its feet that they can take the place of hands. So too the manuscript Arabic translator, who has here العنكبوت [al-ʿankabūt], the spider. To this interpretation Santes, Arias, Mercerus, Munster, Castalio, Junius, Tremellius, the English, Italian and Genevan versions, and any other more recent translators subscribe with complete agreement. But these men, by far the most skilled in the Hebrew language, ought to have observed that nowhere, neither in Scripture nor in the writings of the ancient Hebrews, is the spider called שממית semamith, but everywhere עכביש accabis, whence the Chaldee עכובית accobith and the Arabic عنكبوت [ʿankabūt] ancabuths, still in use today. Moreover, I admit that the feet of spiders are sometimes called fingers, as in the Frogs of Aristophanes, Act 5, [II, 511] Εἰλίσσετε δακτύλοις φάλαγγες ἰσότονα πηνίσματα [Eilissete daktylois phalanges isotona pēnismata],
Twist with your fingers, o spiders, the threads by which the weaver's beam is stretched. And in Ovid's Metamorphoses, book 6, fable 2,
Thin fingers cling to her sides in place of legs.

Τίς τοὺς ἀράχνας λεπτοδακτύλους πλάσας, Νήθειν διδάσκει, καὶ πρὸς ἔργα τοὺς μίτους Ἐκ τῶν παρ᾽ αὐτοῖς ἐντέρων ἀναπτύειν; [Tis tous arachnas leptodaktylous plasas, Nēthein didaskei, kai pros erga tous mitous Ek tōn par' autois enterōn anaptyein?]

Who teaches the spiders, made with slender fingers, to spin, and to spit out threads for their works from their own entrails? But one cannot find anyone who attributes hands to them. For although the spider's feet imitate fingers after a fashion, there is nothing in them that approaches the form of hands. Indeed, in Symphosius, Riddle 17, the spider expressly denies that it has any hands:
I have no hand, yet everything is done by my feet.

But granting, without conceding, that the spider's feet can be taken for hands because they perform the office of hands, the Divine Writer would still not have said that it takes hold with its hands, but that it spins, or weaves, or draws out threads: for that it handles and grasps with its feet is a slight matter, and shared with many animals; that it weaves is peculiar and θαυματῶδες [thaumatōdes]. Nor would he have said that it is in kings' palaces, since the filth of spiders does not well suit the elegance of a royal court. They rather dwell in the house of poor Euclio, in which
— — — there is nothing for thieves to gain, so filled is it with emptiness and spiders.

As Plautus writes in the Aulularia. Everyone knows the fable of the gout and the spider, who, they say, agreed that the former should dwell in the palaces of the rich and the latter in the hovels of the poor. Accordingly, when someone is said to have spiders in his house, or in his chest, or in his vessels, or in his purse, it is the same as saying that he lives in slender circumstances. Hence Afranius in Festus:
Is your little chest so full of spiders?
And Catullus, excusing himself to Fabullus for entertaining him, invited to dinner, less sumptuously:
